title: e2e-latency-profiling-traces-2026-03-25
content:
Summary:
This doc contains end-to-end latency profiling traces collected from the hosted inference tier (prod-like load) during the testing window 2026-03-23 to 2026-03-24. Goal: quantify p50/p95/p99 E2E latency, provide per-stage breakdowns, highlight regressions vs baseline, and recommend mitigations.

Test configuration:
- Model: open-rlhf-13B-v1 (optimized kernels enabled)
- Instance type: g5.12xlarge equivalent (NVLink region)
- Serving runtime: v1.18.3 (commit 3f8a7e)
- Traffic profile: synthetic single-turn generation, avg prompt tokens=42, response tokens=128, request rate 120 rps distributed across 4 AZs
- Batcher config: max_batch_size=64, max_batch_wait_ms=20, dynamic_batching=on
- KV cache: enabled; cache hit rate measured ~78% during run
- Measurement: client->ingress->routing->batcher queuing->inference (kernel exec + decode)->serialize->client; traces captured with distributed tracing (x-trace-id) and high-resolution timestamps

Key metrics (E2E observed):
- E2E latency (client send -> client receive): p50=120 ms, p95=310 ms, p99=640 ms
- Baseline (2026-02-20): p50=110 ms, p95=260 ms, p99=520 ms (notable regression at p95/p99)

Per-stage p50/p95/p99 breakdown (ms):
Stage                        | p50  | p95  | p99
-----------------------------|------|------|-----
Client serialization         |  3   |  6   |  10
Ingress (TLS/parsing/auth)   |  8   | 18   |  28
Routing / policy check       |  5   | 12   |  18
Batcher queue wait           | 20   |120   |200  
Model inference (exec+decode)| 75   |140   |380  
KV-cache miss penalty (extra)|  0   | 10   | 50  
Serialize/egress             |  4   |  6   |  8
Total (measured)             |120   |310   |640  

Notes on numbers:
- The p99 delta vs baseline (~+120 ms) is primarily accounted for by increased batcher queue wait (+~80-100 ms) and a bump in heavy-model p99 inference times (+~60-100 ms).
- KV-cache misses contribute to the long tail for some traces: p99 includes a subset of requests where cache missed warm prefix leading to extra attention-kernel warmup + memory copies (~30-40 ms).

Representative trace excerpts (anonymized x-trace-ids):
- trace-id: x-trace-8a3f5 - 2026-03-24T14:12:03.123Z
  - client_send: 2026-03-24T14:12:03.123Z
  - ingress_received: 2026-03-24T14:12:03.130Z (7 ms)
  - routed_to_pool: 2026-03-24T14:12:03.142Z (12 ms)
  - batcher_enqueue: 2026-03-24T14:12:03.142Z
  - batcher_dequeue/start_exec: 2026-03-24T14:12:03.342Z (200 ms queue wait)
  - model_exec_start: 2026-03-24T14:12:03.342Z
  - model_exec_end: 2026-03-24T14:12:03.712Z (370 ms inference)
  - serialize_end/client_receive: 2026-03-24T14:12:03.720Z (8 ms)
  - total: 597 ms (this trace had a KV-cache miss adding ~40-50 ms in the early exec path)

- trace-id: x-trace-21c9a - 2026-03-24T15:07:11.001Z (p50 example)
  - batcher_queue_wait: 18 ms
  - inference: 76 ms
  - total: 112 ms

Distribution observations:
- Batcher waiting time shows a heavy right tail when request concurrency across AZs spikes transiently (we observe short bursts where per-AZ influx exceeds pre-configured burst tokens).
- Inference kernel latencies at p99 increased after commit 3f8a7e (kernel selector change + newer cuDNN). The majority of heavy p99 traces align with model-decoder kernel fallbacks that choose a slower path for longer sequences (>120 tokens).
- KV cache hit rate at 78% is okay, but the 22% misses correlate with larger-than-average upstream requests and cause additional memory transfer/setup time.

Hypothesis / Root cause analysis:
1) Increased p99 is a combination of batching queueing during short traffic bursts and a small fraction of inference requests falling into a slower kernel path for long outputs. Both effects compound: queued requests then hit the slower kernel, amplifying the tail.
2) Recent runtime change (commit 3f8a7e) introduced a kernel-selection heuristic tweak that moves borderline workloads to a safer (but slower) execution path on some hardware. This accounts for the kernel-related portion of the regression.
3) Batcher configuration (max_batch_wait_ms=20) allows larger queues under 20ms window; with higher concurrency the queue builds and p95/p99 increase.

Recommended mitigations (short -> medium term):
- Short term (hours):
  - Reduce max_batch_wait_ms from 20 -> 10 for the affected pool to reduce queue tail. Monitor throughput and unit cost impact. Owner: Asha Patel. ETA: 24h.
  - Pin kernel selector to previous heuristic for g5-like fleet to validate regression rollback (hotfix branch). Owner: Noah Singh. ETA: 48h.
- Medium term (days):
  - Implement adaptive batching (batch_timeout scales with observed queue length) to avoid fixed window tail behavior. Owner: Liam Chen. ETA: 5 days.
  - Improve kernel fallback telemetry: add tags to traces when slower kernel is chosen to make aggregation easier. Owner: Marta Ruiz. ETA: 3 days.
  - Add aggressive pre-warm for KV cache for long-prefix workloads (pre-fetch top-k prefixes during cold starts). Owner: Asha Patel. ETA: 7 days.
- Long term (weeks):
  - Revisit kernel-selection heuristics with more A/B testing across sequence length distributions and hardware profiles. Owner: Serving-runtime team. ETA: 3+ weeks.
  - Autoscaler tuning: ensure rapid scale-out on short spikes (reduce cool-down, increase burst tokens) to limit per-AZ queueing. Owner: Platform-engineering. ETA: 2 weeks.

Action items (tracking):
- JIRA-1973: reduce max_batch_wait_ms and monitor (Asha) — in progress
- CONFS-4821: kernel selector rollback experiment + perf tests (Noah) — blocked by infra
- PR #842: adaptive batching prototype (Liam) — WIP

Instrumentation notes / next steps for data collection:
- Tag traces with kernel-path and kv-cache-hit boolean (already added to proto; need rollout to all fleets).
- Collect per-batch histogram: batch size vs queue wait vs downstream p99.
- Run focused load test with elevated long-seq ratio (increase response tokens to 256) to reproduce kernel fallback more reliably.

Appendix — quick heatmap summary (observed):
- When per-AZ qps > 35, batcher p95 > 150 ms  (clustered bursts in 15–30s windows)
- Kernel fallback traces account for ~6% of requests but represent ~40% of p99 tail cost

Conclusions:
- Current p50 is acceptable but p95/p99 regressions are real and measurable. Immediate reduction of batch wait window and a rollback/experiment of kernel selector reduce the long tail while we build more adaptive batching and kernel-selection telemetry.

Comments and open questions (notes to self / team):
- Need to confirm cost impact of reducing max_batch_wait_ms for dedicated customers — present numbers for trade-off.
- Should we expose batch wait as a per-customer knob in Dedicated offering? pros/cons.
